## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Sessions 2–3: describe and compare curves
- Today: **regression for survival**: effect sizes, adjustment for several variables
- By the end you can:
  - fit a **Cox model** and interpret a **hazard ratio** and its CI
  - fit and report a **multivariable** model
  - **scale** continuous variables and check **events per variable**
  - draw a **predicted survival curve** for a patient profile
:::

# Topic 1 — The hazard ratio {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## The model

::: {.eq}
h(t | x) = h~0~(t) × exp(β~1~x~1~ + β~2~x~2~ + …)
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **h~0~(t)** is an unspecified **baseline hazard**: the shape over time is left free
- **exp(β)** is the **hazard ratio**: the **multiplicative** change in the hazard for a one-unit increase in x, **at any time**
- **Proportional hazards:** that ratio is **constant over time** (checked in Session 5)
- Like logistic regression it uses **exp(coefficient)**, but it models **rates over time**
:::

## One predictor

```{r}
cox1 <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hiv, data = tb)
exp(cbind(HR = coef(cox1), confint(cox1))) |> round(2)
```

::: {.key}
**HR = `r round(exp(coef(cox1)), 2)`** (95% CI `r round(exp(confint(cox1))[1], 1)`–`r round(exp(confint(cox1))[2], 1)`): at any time, the **hazard of death is about `r round(100 * (exp(coef(cox1)) - 1))`% higher** in HIV-positive patients. It is a **rate ratio, not a risk ratio**; and unlike the log-rank test it has a **size and a CI**.
:::

# Topic 2 — Adjusted model {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Several predictors at once

```{r}
cox_full <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ age + sex + hiv + diabetes + smoker + bmi + mdr_tb + treatment, data = tb)
round(exp(cbind(HR = coef(cox_full), confint(cox_full))), 2)    # tbl_regression(cox_full, exponentiate = TRUE) formats this for a paper
```

## Reading the adjusted hazard ratios

::: {.incremental}
- Each HR is **adjusted for the others**: "holding age, sex, … fixed"
- **MDR-TB** about doubles the hazard; **DOT** about halves it (reference: self-administered); sex shows no effect
- The **CI** shows the precision: a CI that includes **1** means no clear association
:::

## Reading continuous predictors

```{r}
cox_age10 <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ I(age / 10) + hiv + mdr_tb + treatment, data = tb)
round(exp(cbind(HR = coef(cox_age10), confint(cox_age10))), 2)[1, ]
```

The HR for age is for **one year** unless you rescale: **per 10 years** is a more readable unit (HR^10). For BMI, use a clinically sensible step (per 5 kg/m²).

## Events per variable

```{r}
c(events = sum(tb$status), coefficients = length(coef(cox_full)), events_per_coefficient = round(sum(tb$status) / length(coef(cox_full)), 1))
```

::: {.warn}
The information in a Cox model is the **number of events**, not the number of patients. As a rule of thumb, aim for **about 10 or more events per coefficient**; with fewer, estimates are unstable and the model overfits. Choose predictors **from theory** first (Session 6 of the regression workshop).
:::

# Topic 3 — Using the model {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Predicted survival for a patient profile

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
nd <- tibble(age = 40, sex = "Male", hiv = c("Negative", "Positive"), diabetes = "No", smoker = "No", bmi = 20, mdr_tb = "No", treatment = "DOT") |>
  mutate(across(c(sex, hiv, diabetes, smoker, mdr_tb, treatment), \(v) factor(v, levels = levels(tb[[cur_column()]]))))
ps <- survfit(cox_full, newdata = nd)
tibble(month = ps$time, hiv_neg = ps$surv[, 1], hiv_pos = ps$surv[, 2]) |> pivot_longer(-month, names_to = "profile", values_to = "survival") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, survival, colour = profile)) + geom_step(linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Months", y = "Predicted survival", colour = NULL)
```

A **40-year-old man on DOT without MDR-TB or diabetes**, HIV-negative vs positive: the model gives the **expected curve** for any covariate pattern.

## HR is not a risk ratio

::: {.incremental}
- An HR of 2 means the **rate** of dying is twice as high **at each moment**, not that the **cumulative risk** is doubled
- With **rare** events they are close; with common events they differ
- Report the HR **and** survival (or risk) at fixed times when possible
:::

## Reporting a Cox model

::: {.good}
- **Events and patients** in each group; **median follow-up**
- **Crude and adjusted HRs with 95% CI** (state the covariates and why)
- The **reference** category and the **unit** of each continuous variable
- The result of the **proportional-hazards check** (Session 5)
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q1", "A Cox model gives HR = 2.0 (95% CI 1.2 to 3.3) for HIV-positive vs negative patients. Which interpretation is correct?",
         c("HIV-positive patients are twice as likely to die during the study",
           "HIV-positive patients survive twice as long as negative patients",
           "At any time, the hazard of death is about twice as high with HIV",
           "Two per cent more HIV-positive patients die in every single month"), answer = 3,
         explain = "A hazard ratio compares instantaneous event rates at any time. It is not a ratio of cumulative risks or of survival times.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q2", "Age has HR = 1.02 per year. What is the approximate HR per 10 years?",
         c("About 1.20, because 0.02 is added 10 times",
           "About 1.22, because 1.02 multiplied by itself 10 times",
           "About 2.0, because 10 years doubles the hazard",
           "About 1.02, since the hazard ratio does not depend on the unit"), answer = 2,
         explain = "Hazard ratios multiply: 1.02^10 ≈ 1.22. The unit of a continuous variable matters, so rescale to a meaningful step.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q3", "Why is the number of events, not the number of patients, the key constraint on a Cox model?",
         c("Each patient appears just one time in the data set used to fit it",
           "Cox models can only use the patients who died during follow-up",
           "Information comes from events; censored patients add at-risk time",
           "Censored patients are removed before the model is fitted to the rest"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Estimating coefficients relies on comparing who has the event with who is at risk. Few events mean unstable estimates, whatever the number of patients.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q4", "In a Cox model the HR for treatment (DOT vs self-administered) is 0.57. What does this say?",
         c("DOT patients have a 57% probability of dying during follow-up",
           "DOT patients live 43% longer than self-administered patients do",
           "The hazard is 0.57 times lower with self-administered treatment",
           "With other variables fixed, hazard of death is about 43% lower"), answer = 4,
         explain = "An HR below 1 is a lower hazard: 1 − 0.57 = 43% lower, adjusted for the other variables in the model, relative to the reference group.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q5", "What is the baseline hazard h0(t) in the Cox model?",
         c("The hazard for a patient with all covariates at reference values",
           "The proportion of patients who died during the follow-up period",
           "The hazard ratio of the first predictor entered into the model",
           "A constant rate that must be estimated before the model is fitted"), answer = 1,
         explain = "The Cox model leaves the shape of h0(t) free, estimating only the hazard ratios. That is why it is called semi-parametric.")
```
